title: Agent Transfer Protocol: Server-Mediated Agent-to-Agent Communication Architecture for the Agentic Web
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Agent Transfer Protocol: Server-Mediated Agent-to-Agent Communication Architecture for the Agentic Web
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:The Agentic Web needs to support continuous collaboration among agents from different organizations. These collaborative relationships may span multiple tasks, network connections and execution instances. Such interactions require stable communication entries, message reception when instances are offline, and source verification after delayed reading. How to organize these responsibilities so that cross domain communication does not depend on specific execution instances being continuously online is a key issue for building long term agent interaction infrastructure. We propose ATP (Agent Transfer Protocol), a cross organization agent communication protocol adopting a domain mediated architecture. In this architecture, administrative domains maintain stable addresses and receiving entries for logical agents. The domain servers of both parties continuously undertake cross domain transmission. The receiving domain verifies and saves messages for execution instances to read later. The sending domain signs the complete message envelope. This allows the receiving instance to independently reverify the domain source and content integrity after the original connection ends, provided the original verification public key is still trusted and obtainable. We implemented an ATP prototype and evaluated it through a controlled cross organization LLM agent workflow, mechanism checks and latency measurements. The workflow completed subsequent business processing after instances went offline or were replaced. The independent verifier successfully verified the domain source and content integrity of saved messages. Latency measurements further quantified the communication and processing overhead introduced by the continuous mediation of domain servers.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper proposes ATP, a domain-mediated protocol that lets AI agents from different organizations exchange signed, stored messages even when their execution instances go offline.
report.background: The push toward an "agentic web" has produced a wave of interoperability work: Anthropic's Model Context Protocol for tool access, Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) for peer tasks, and various academic schemes for multi-agent negotiation. Most of these assume agents are addressable and live at the moment of interaction — typically an HTTP request/response or a streaming session. But real cross-organizational collaboration spans many tasks, machines and restarts. Agents get redeployed, spot instances are killed, and network sessions drop. Existing designs also struggle with identity: if a message arrives hours late, how does the receiver know which organization truly sent it? ATP borrows the older, proven email model — stable organizational addresses, store-and-forward relays, and cryptographic signatures on the whole envelope — and adapts it to LLM-driven agent workflows.
key_points: Stable addresses, not live processes: Administrative domains hold a permanent address and inbox for each logical agent. Execution instances come and go, but the agent remains reachable, so collaboration can survive restarts, redeployments and offline periods without the sender having to know anything about the receiver's runtime.

Domain servers act as continuous relays: Instead of one direct peer-to-peer connection, the sending and receiving domains' servers handle cross-domain transmission. The receiving domain verifies each message and stores it until an instance is available to read it, mirroring how SMTP mail servers hold messages.

Envelope-level signatures enable delayed verification: The sending domain signs the complete message envelope, so a receiving instance can independently re-verify the domain of origin and content integrity long after the original connection closed — provided the original verification key is still trusted and retrievable.

Prototype validated on a real workflow: The authors built an ATP implementation and ran a controlled cross-organization LLM agent workflow. Business processing completed successfully even after the original instances went offline or were replaced, and an independent verifier confirmed source and integrity of stored messages.

Latency costs quantified: Measurements captured the overhead introduced by continuous domain-server mediation, giving an early empirical baseline for the trade-off between reliability and speed in agent messaging infrastructure.
report.impact: ATP reframes agent communication from a networking problem into an infrastructure problem, closer to email than to RPC. For the AI industry, that suggests a layered stack: agent frameworks on top, protocols like MCP and A2A for interaction semantics, and something like ATP underneath for durable, verifiable delivery. For developers, it implies agent identity and message signing become first-class concerns — you would design agents as long-lived logical entities with keys and inboxes, not just processes with endpoints. There is a cost: mediation adds latency and makes domain servers a trust and availability chokepoint. For regular users, the payoff is reliability — long-running tasks that survive closed laptops or crashed sessions, plus clearer proof of which company's agent actually sent a message.
report.tools: Watch Google's A2A and Anthropic's MCP roadmaps, since ATP is complementary rather than competing. For hands-on experimentation, JWS/JOSE libraries and DID-based key infrastructure cover envelope signing and verification; LiteLLM, LangGraph or Microsoft AutoGen provide agent runtimes to wire into a relay; a plain SMTP/IMAP-style mailbox or NATS/Redis queue can prototype store-and-forward quickly. The arXiv paper's prototype is the best reference implementation to follow, alongside the AGNTCY agent-directory efforts.
